extracted.intended_audience: criminal judges, forensic psychologists, and criminalists assessing testimony and motive (historical/clinical guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for judges and criminal psychologists on how physiological (menstruation, pregnancy), erotic, and concealed sexual factors affect women's perception, testimony, and criminal behavior, and how to investigate and interpret those influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check menstrual status at time of perception and testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Discover whether the child/woman was passing through her monthly period at the time when she saw the event under discussion, or when she was telling about it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If menstruating at time of the event, she may have told of more than could have been perceived; if menstruating at time of testimony, she may develop the delusion that she had seen more than she really had. Newly menstruating girls’ false statements tend to be romantic, extraordinary, and interesting. Examine witnesses who know her prior trustworthiness; re‑examine, and if necessary call in medical aid. Be cautious: direct questions are often answered falsely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for intensified sensibility during menstruation
rubrics_metrics.description: Menstrual period tends to modify the quality of perception and the truth of description; senses (especially skin/touch, smell, hearing) can be intensified during menses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that a menstruating woman may have perceived things others would not at another time; be mindful of the boundary between delicate perception and over-excitability. This can make witnesses, victims, and accused more emotionally reactive and produce altered testimony or complaints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of trials relative to menstrual cycles
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that complaints by menstruating women often recur in a cycle; trials conducted exactly four weeks after the crime or accusation may coincide with the same state of excitement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid holding crucial hearings or taking testimony at times that correspond to the woman's typical menstrual-related excitability; consider timing to reduce periodic bias in complaints or testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider menstruation as contributing factor to anger, falsification, theft, and transient psychoses
rubrics_metrics.description: Menstruation can incline some women to anger and falsification, and disturbances of menstruation can lead to abnormal, sometimes transient psychoses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a woman's testimony or conduct is significant and unconfirmed, consider menstrual influence; if suspected, re-examination, corroboration, and medical assessment are appropriate. Historical reports (e.g., shoplifting clusters at onset of menses) are cited as illustrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Call physician and consider somatic/psychic effects of pregnancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Pregnancy powerfully influences the psychic life of a woman and may produce desires, conduct, impulses, and subtle alterations of viewpoint that affect testimony and behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In cases of crimes committed by pregnant women or important testimony from pregnant women, call a physician. Ask about the impression the event made on her, since subjective attitude during pregnancy may alter description and lead to objective falsehood even without deliberate lying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask about and interpret witness’s subjective impression and point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: A witness’s statement always contains judgment and depends on her point of view, which varies with emotional state (e.g., pregnancy, menstruation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question witnesses about whether an attack seemed dangerous, insulting, premeditated, etc., to understand their perspective. If only one witness exists, recognize the risk that subjective attitude may go uncorrected and lead to erroneous conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Count maternal instinct and sexual impulse in explaining behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Variations in sexual sensibility and the maternal instinct can explain accommodation to men's desires, sexual impropriety, or other criminal phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume a single standard of female sexual impulse; consider maternal instinct as a factor in domestic relations, motives toward husband/children, and certain crimes. Evaluate how social/civilizational conditions might suppress or alter this instinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek submerged sexual motives when surface motives are absent or inadequate
rubrics_metrics.description: Hidden sexual impulses often underlie acts where motive is unclear; shame causes these motives to operate covertly, especially in women.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the causal chain from disposition to crime is obscure, explore concealed sexual grounds that may be disguised under other motives. Remember motive (conscious) vs ground (deeper influences) distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use religiosity/ostentatious piety as a probe for concealed sexuality
rubrics_metrics.description: False piety and ostentatious religious behavior can be a mask covering hidden sexual passion or sensuality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate exhibited religiosity (e.g., setting up altars, compelling others to pray) as potential evidence of concealed sexual interests. Such signs are often easier to observe and corroborate than direct sexual impulses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat sudden or intensified conceit as indicator of sexual interest or change
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceit (vanity) may function as a sexual characteristic; sudden increases in conceit can indicate pursuit of a lover or heightened sexual attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether a woman has a lover, when conceit first began, and whether it relates to a particular man. If these conditions are confirmed, inference about sexual motivation or influence on behavior may be strong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider ennui (boredom) as a marker for erotic dissatisfaction and possible criminal predisposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Ennui is an emotional state—often rooted in sexual energy—that can prompt a range of misdeeds from petty thefts to grave crimes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inquire into periods of boredom noted by neighbors or acquaintances and the onset of criminal thoughts or plans during such periods. Treat reported or observed ennui as a substantive clue to motive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe displays of new goods/adornment as evidence of theft
rubrics_metrics.description: Women commonly reveal ill-gotten gains quickly by wearing or displaying them, making detection more likely than for men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When theft is suspected, check whether the accused or her associates are suddenly displaying new clothing, jewelry, or ornaments. Historical anecdotal evidence suggests this is a reliable investigative heuristic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infer hidden sexual motives via intermediate, observable traits rather than direct questioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct questions about sensual inclinations are almost always worthless; better to ask about religious activity, piety, conceit, dress, and behavior that are openly exhibited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use corroborated, observable signs to infer concealed impulses. Avoid reliance on self-reports of sexual motive; instead, build the case from external, confirmable behaviors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroborate testimony with acquaintances for prior truthfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: To assess whether menstrual or other periodic conditions influenced testimony, examine persons who knew the woman's earlier trustworthiness and love of truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If witnesses confirm preexisting tendencies toward exaggeration or untruthfulness, this strengthens the suspicion of influence by menstrual or psychical conditions. Use such testimony to decide on re-examination or medical assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be alert to periodic/transient psychoses linked to menstrual or gestational disturbance
rubrics_metrics.description: Disturbances of menstruation or pregnancy may precipitate abnormal psychoses that develop quietly and may be overlooked if labeled mere 'nervous excitement.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When behavior suggests transient mental disease, secure a medical/psychiatric assessment rather than assuming mere emotional agitation. Such conditions may materially affect criminal responsibility and testimony reliability.
